topic: DOE FY2027 budget increase and agency funding priorities
summary: DOE presented a proposed FY 2027 budget of about 5.58 billion, an increase of 25.74%, and attributed it mainly to gray geometry, mobile energy systems, and automation. Members questioned the increase, DOE’s 49% obligation rate, the separate emergency allotment of about 29 billion, and whether the projects would deliver lower rates, fewer outages, and lasting electrification. DOE said the projects would improve energy security, committed to provide fuel-marking data, and described plans for government-controlled strategic petroleum storage. ERC requested more than 700 million, or at least about 200 million plus, to complete distribution-utility rate resets, while NEA sought 7 or 10 billion to cushion electric cooperatives from system-loss elimination. Members broadly supported DOE and ERC, but final restorations and special provisions were left to subcommittee review, DBM consultation, committee action, and plenary.
question: The committee sought to establish why DOE’s FY 2027 budget was increasing by roughly 25%, whether its existing and emergency resources were being properly utilized, and whether the proposed funding would improve energy security, electricity reliability, and consumer prices. Members also examined related unfunded priorities, ERC’s request for additional resources, system-loss reduction, and the development of government-controlled fuel reserves.
agency_position: DOE maintained that its proposed increase was concentrated in three energy-security and modernization projects—gray geometry, mobile energy systems, and automation—and that it did not seek a further increase beyond the proposed budget. DOE supported additional ERC resources for rate resets and a strong regulator, while seeking special provisions and corporate-fund authority for energy-security measures. The agencies committed to provide utilization, fuel-marking, strategic-reserve, system-loss, and ERC funding details, but several requests remained subject to budget-subcommittee, DBM, committee, and plenary action.
outcome: The committee generally supported DOE’s proposed budget and endorsed stronger ERC funding, but did not finally resolve the additional ERC, NEA, DOE special-provision, or reserve-related requests. DOE and ERC were directed to submit detailed information for review by the budget amendments review subcommittee, with DBM consultations and plenary action still required.

thread.said: DOE said it was using 500,000,000 from current appropriations and 21,000,000 from continuing appropriations for mobile energy systems in 2026, and was proposing 600,000,000 in 2027 for at least 60 additional units. thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon Garin

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon Garin

topic: System-loss reduction, anti-pilferage, and electric-cooperative funding
summary: Rep. Chukwish questioned ERC on the VAT treatment of the 12% system-loss charge and when consumers would see changes, while ERC said the BIR process and publication requirements had to be completed. DOE and ERC distinguished technical from nontechnical losses, described four phases of twenty five percent reductions for nontechnical losses, and said cooperatives needed about six months to prepare technical-loss plans. ERC identified November as the earliest hoped-for billing implementation and later clarified that the 7,500,000,000 figure was for nontechnical-loss work, with cooperative assistance to be assessed case by case. Members also pressed for cooperative subsidy reforms, safeguards against rooftop-solar costs being shifted to non-solar consumers, and action on stranded capacity. ERC requested more than 700 million and at least about 200 million for consulting and related operating expenses, while NEA requested 7 or 10 billion to cushion cooperatives; the chair approved the ERC request and the 8.2 reconsideration amount for NEA CTO electrification, although the unit of the latter figure was unclear. The agencies committed to further guidelines, consultations, cooperative assessments, and studies, but final funding and technical-loss obligations remained open.
question: The committee sought to establish how technical and nontechnical system losses would be reduced, how their VAT and billing treatment would affect consumers, and how the effort would be financed without shifting costs to consumers or destabilizing electric cooperatives. Members also asked about cooperative subsidies, rooftop solar, stranded costs, and the adequacy of DOE, ERC, and NEA funding.
agency_position: DOE, ERC, and NEA stated that nontechnical losses, particularly pilferage, should be eliminated through phased enforcement, consumer education, billing improvements, and cooperative support, with a stated objective of zero nontechnical loss and implementation potentially within one year. They said technical-loss reduction required cooperative-specific engineering plans and could not be rushed; funding would be assessed case by case and, where possible, obtained from cooperative earnings, loans, or existing resources rather than additional national funding.
outcome: The agencies provided a phased plan and timetable, including a possible November billing implementation and a one-year objective for eliminating nontechnical losses. Funding, technical-loss targets for private utilities, the final treatment of VAT and stranded costs, and the adequacy of NEA support remained subject to further guidelines, studies, consultations, and budget action.

Demanded the policy basis and fiscal-space implications of eliminating technical and nontechnical losses, while questioning whether private utilities would comply.
Urged ERC to address stranded costs and excess contracted capacity so that solar adoption would benefit consumers rather than leave costs with captive customers.

topic: ERC budget reduction, restoration, and regulatory capacity
summary: The ERC chair presented a workload that included thousands of decisions and orders, rate resets after more than a decade, and system-loss regulation, while saying the FY 2027 allocation was below the commission's proposal. The ERC sought restoration of more than 700,000,000, or at least around 200,000,000 plus for consultants and related operating expenses. Secretary Sharon Garin and Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported stronger ERC funding, with Rodriguez also referring to a 120,000,000 increase. NEA separately requested 7 or 10,000,000,000 to cushion electric cooperatives from nontechnical system-loss elimination. The committee chair asked for detailed justification and a prioritized list, and the ERC committed to submit a narrative explaining the consultancy requirement and its link to rate resets and system-loss reduction. No final restoration amount was adopted during the hearing; DBM-related special-provision questions were deferred for discussion before plenary.
question: The committee sought to establish why the ERC's FY 2027 funding was reduced, how much additional funding was needed to sustain its regulatory workload, and whether the requested resources were tied to specific outputs such as rate resets and system-loss reduction. It also sought to determine what documentation the ERC would provide to support restoration or augmentation of its budget.
agency_position: The ERC said its workload and regulatory responsibilities had expanded substantially, while its available FY 2027 funding was below its proposal. It sought restoration of more than 700,000,000, or at minimum around 200,000,000 plus for consultants and related operating expenses, to complete utility rate resets in 2027 and support system-loss reduction and eventual removal of system-loss charges.
outcome: The committee expressed support for restoring or augmenting the ERC budget but did not record a final appropriation in the hearing. The ERC was required to submit detailed justifications and a prioritized list for review by the budget amendments review subcommittee, while the special-provision issue remained subject to consultation with DBM.

topic: Electricity supply security, alerts, outages, and reserve capacity
summary: The Chair and members examined whether the proposed DOE and ERC resources would prevent future alerts, outages, fuel shortages, and high-cost generation. DOE attributed the Visayas and Mindanao alerts to coinciding maintenance, defective coal-plant equipment, reduced hydropower and biomass output, and forced operation of remaining plants, while proposing up to 250 megawatts of Visayas battery storage and short-term deployment of about 200 to 300 megawatts. Members also questioned Iligan's reduced 8.75 megawatt firm allocation, DOE's 49% utilization rate, the excluded 29,000,000,000 emergency allotment, and the adequacy of government-controlled fuel reserves. DOE and PNOC described plans for a government-owned 1,000,000-barrel tank farm, while the reported national fuel inventory remained largely in private storage. ERC said it would address excess contracted capacity and review reserve-market pricing, but several allocation, outage, CBA, system-loss, and stranded-cost issues remained open. The committee requested written fuel and remittance reports and carried the matters forward for subsequent action.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 DOE and ERC resources would improve electricity supply security, reduce alerts and outages, secure fuel and reserves, and prevent consumers from bearing the cost of excess or unreliable generation. Members also asked what immediate and long-term measures would address constrained Visayas and Mindanao supply, plant outages, battery storage, firm-power allocations, and strategic petroleum reserves.
agency_position: DOE and ERC maintained that the proposed programs would strengthen energy security through resource surveys, mobile energy systems, automation, battery storage, renewable integration, improved monitoring, and strategic fuel reserves. DOE attributed current alerts mainly to coinciding maintenance, defective equipment, reduced hydropower and biomass output, and forced operation of remaining plants, while ERC said market and contract mechanisms could mitigate congestion, excess capacity, and reserve-market costs.
outcome: The committee received explanations and several forward commitments, but the underlying supply-security problems were not fully resolved. DOE and PNOC committed to written reports, battery deployment, plant monitoring, system-loss work, and development of government-controlled fuel storage; Iligan's added allocation, the CBA memorandum, stranded costs, and the full impact of outages remained subject to further action.

topic: Strategic petroleum reserve, fuel storage, and emergency fuel allotments
summary: The Chair framed the energy budget as requiring permanent preparedness after DOE secured more than 178 million liters of diesel for an emergency buffer. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos questioned DOE's separate emergency allotment of 29,860,000,000 and asked how much fuel the government actually controlled. DOE said an additional 29,000,000,000 had been passed to PNOC and would be separately liquidated after the emergency, but it did not provide a clear government-controlled days-of-supply figure. DOE undertook to provide data comparing fuel imports and sales to help assess illicit fuel and fuel-marking gaps. PNOC said it would begin with a 1,000,000-barrel tank farm and later expand it, while Sharon Garin said construction could be completed in a year and a half and would require about 8,000,000,000. Members supported the need for a strategic reserve, but the final government-controlled capacity and the inconsistent later-phase figures were left open.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the Philippines had a government-controlled strategic petroleum reserve, how much emergency fuel was under government control, where fuel was stored, and how the reserve would be financed and expanded. Members also asked how DOE measured illicit fuel, whether private commercial storage was sufficient, and what documents or infrastructure commitments would follow.
agency_position: DOE said the emergency fuel allotment was being retained and would be liquidated separately after the emergency ended. It supported a permanent, government-owned strategic petroleum reserve through PNOC, beginning with a 1,000,000-barrel tank farm and expanding through later phases, while acknowledging that current national storage figures largely reflected private commercial facilities. DOE also said it would provide import-versus-sales and fuel-marking data and use cross-agency data analysis to address illicit-fuel gaps.
outcome: The agency committed to developing a PNOC-owned strategic reserve, beginning with a 1,000,000-barrel facility and scaling up, but did not provide a final figure for government-controlled days of supply. DOE also undertook to submit fuel-marking and import-versus-sales data; the extent of government control, the later-phase reserve size, and the financing details remained partly unresolved.

positions.position: The energy sector should receive sustained, measurable support, with the emergency response converted into funded and operational strategic fuel-reserve and storage capabilities.

DOE should account for emergency resources separately and transparently, determine how much fuel is under government control, and establish a genuine government-owned reserve rather than relying only on emergency purchases or private storage. He nevertheless manifested support for the DOE budget and additional consumer-protection funding.
The country should maintain a diesel reserve and develop storage under government control so it is less exposed to foreign supply disruptions and private-company dependence.
DOE should clarify foreign-linked fuel-storage projects and ensure that the Philippines' finite storage capacity and permitting authority are properly addressed.

topic: Total electrification and off-grid solar, batteries, and fuel support
summary: DOE presented Mobile Energy Systems and a proposed 2027 allocation of about 600 million for at least 60 units, while members questioned whether much larger resources were needed to close the remaining electrification gap. Rep. Nassal was told that total electrification required roughly 8 to 10 billion annually, compared with receipts of about 2 to 3 billion, although parts of the household and timeline figures were garbled. Rep. Stephen Tan raised an approved but unfunded off-grid solar project, fuel shortages, pole relocation, submarine-cable resilience and solar-plant fees; DOE and NEA undertook follow-up actions. Rep. Jan Chan pressed for targeting high-poverty and geographically isolated areas, while DOE and NEA said Mindanao and disadvantaged areas were priorities but did not provide exact regional allocations. The chair approved reconsideration of additional CTO-electrification funding after NEA confirmed the figures cited for its proposal and grant. A minority member also proposed a 200 million solar-and-battery alternative to line extensions, receiving agreement in principle but no recorded implementation details.
question: The committee sought to establish how the proposed budget would accelerate total electrification, particularly in off-grid, geographically isolated and high-poverty areas, and whether solar-battery systems could substitute for costly line extensions. Members also asked what funding, fuel support, infrastructure and policy changes DOE, NEA and related agencies would provide.
agency_position: DOE and NEA supported accelerating total electrification through the Total Electrification Program, Mobile Energy Systems, photovoltaic mainstreaming, solar-home systems and solar-plus-battery projects, while recognizing that funding remained insufficient. The agencies favored targeted deployment in Mindanao, geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, and high-poverty communities, but several site-specific funding, fuel, fee-waiver and infrastructure questions required follow-up.
outcome: The hearing produced commitments to follow up on specific off-grid solar, fuel, pole-relocation, submarine-cable and transmission concerns, and the chair approved reconsideration of additional CTO-electrification funding for Mindanao. The broader funding requirement, exact number and cost of remaining CTOs and households, poverty-targeted allocations, and the proposed 200,000,000 solar-battery provision were not fully resolved in the transcript.

positions.position: Supported expressly authorizing DOE to access legally earmarked special-fund revenues, provided DOE clearly identified lawful programs, and supported increasing resources for total electrification.

Pressed for funding of approved off-grid solar, adequate fuel allocation for islands, pole-relocation assistance, resilient submarine connections, fee relief for a donor-supported solar plant and faster Visayas transmission development.

Called for electrification resources to be targeted to regions with high absolute poverty and poverty incidence, and sought continued support for offshore-wind development and related port and grid infrastructure.
Supported reconsideration of the gap between NEA's CTO-electrification request and the amount in the NEP, particularly for Mindanao, and approved the reconsideration during the hearing.
Advocated changing the CSP and electrification framework to allow solar panels and battery storage, after technical and economic evaluation, instead of extending lines to some rural areas.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: DOE asked for the island's name and said the matter could be checked, particularly if it was a SPUG area. The official also suggested redesigning the system to reduce dependence on diesel.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: The NEA administrator said he would meet with the relevant secretary on pole relocation and had requested at least 300,000,000 to cover electric-cooperative advances. He said 2026 DPWH allocation was 50,000,000 and promised to place the lane-expansion relocations high on the list.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: Tan asked whether an island approximately 1.5 kilometers from the mainland could be connected through a submarine cable rather than overhead poles to improve resilience during typhoons.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: DOE said a submarine cable was possible but required a cost-benefit analysis. If it was not viable, another technology would be considered, and the agency would discuss the matter with Tan's team.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: Tan asked whether fees of roughly 100,000 a month could be waived for a solar project in SAMELCO I that had received roughly 60,000,000 in European Union assistance.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: NEA said it would check the status of the charges. The administrator noted that collections or spending might be needed to cover operation and maintenance of the solar plant.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: Tan asked about upgrading the Luzon-Visayas transmission line to avoid power shedding in Regions 8 and 6, noting that the plan reportedly placed the upgrade in 2032.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary Sharon Garrin
thread.said: DOE said it was developing a Visayas energy master plan after completing work for Mindoro and Palawan. The agency said each major island might need to become more independent in its energy supply rather than relying continually on inter-island connections, and promised to present the plan after another month of simulation.

thread.speaker: NAPOCOR president Coco Nograles
thread.said: Nograles said the island had sufficient generators but was operating for eight hours. NAPOCOR committed to study the economics of increasing service; current peak demand was 108 kilowatts.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jan Franz Chan
thread.said: Chan asked how NEA would apply the proposed poverty-targeting provision in the 2027 rollout and how many CTO energization projects would be located in regions with the highest poverty counts, including Bicol.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: DOE said it had directed NEA to prioritize Mindanao, while the NEA administrator would provide further information on Bicol.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: NEA said its direction covered geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas and that most SEP funding had been dedicated to Mindanao. It mentioned Region 5 and areas including Albay, but did not provide exact regional figures.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary Sharon Garrin
thread.said: DOE said it was revising guidelines to increase host-community benefits from one centavo per kilowatt to three centavos per kilowatt and to give the host cooperative a right of first refusal in the competitive selection process.

thread.speaker: Rep. Jan Franz Chan
thread.said: Chan asked whether the administration still supported a Philippine energy-plan target of 21 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2040, supplying about 21% of electricity, and what budget support was needed for ports and grid preparation.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary Sharon Garrin
thread.said: The secretary could not confirm the percentage target but said DOE continued to push offshore wind and was conducting another energy-mix simulation. She said a final mix would be issued at the end of the year and would still include offshore wind.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: An agency official said the offshore-wind green-energy auction was ongoing for 3,300 megawatts.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator Daniel Mehta
thread.said: Mehta said line extensions to unserved and unviable CTOs could increase technical system losses, but the energy family was working to contain and eventually eliminate nontechnical system losses.

thread.speaker: DOE secretary Sharon Garrin
thread.said: DOE said it was scheduling a Mindanao green-energy auction combining solar with batteries and had directed NEA to prioritize Mindanao energization. DOE said additional available resources should also support Mindanao and transmission improvements.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator Daniel Mehta
thread.said: Mehta said the NEP granted NEA 55,000,000,000, then corrected or clarified the figure as 5,000,000,000, the same amount as the prior year, including photovoltaic mainstreaming. He expressed concern that eliminating nontechnical system losses could financially strain electric cooperatives.

thread.speaker: Chair Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: The chair stated that NEA had proposed 11,200,000,000 for CTO electrification but had been given 2.9, leaving 8.2 for reconsideration. The NEA administrator confirmed the figures, and the chair said the reconsideration was approved.

thread.speaker: minority member
thread.said: A minority member proposed that, after economic and technical evaluation, solar panels and battery storage be used instead of line extensions in rural areas served by electric cooperatives.

thread.speaker: minority member
thread.said: The member proposed 200,000,000 for the solar-and-battery alternative and asked that the special provision permit use of the technology for electrification.

thread.speaker: committee chair and agency officials
thread.said: The proposal to use new technology instead of line extensions was met with agreement during the hearing, although no detailed implementing language or allocation was recorded.

topic: Transmission upgrades, congestion charges, and NGCP reliability
summary: Members raised concerns that inadequate firm power, delayed transmission projects, congestion charges, and NGCP performance were contributing to high rates and reliability risks. PISAM said Iligan's allocation had fallen because Agus and Pulangui dependable capacity declined and committed to evaluate an increase from 8.75 megawatt toward the requested 25 megawatt. DOE and Transco cited planned or proposed connections for Catanduanes and Eastern Samar, a Visayas master plan, storage, and third-party construction, but several projects remained subject to funding and approvals. ERC said LLCC suspension applied only during congested trading intervals and committed to review disputed collections. Transco reported roughly 160,000 right-of-way claims and an estimated 220,000,000,000 settlement cost, with a target to settle 50,000 claims in two years and clear them by 2034. Members also obtained commitments for the PNPP1 feasibility study, NGCP performance and dividend records, and updates on Negros-Panay Line 2 and CNP approval.
question: The committee sought to establish whether transmission constraints, congestion charges, delayed interconnections, and NGCP performance were contributing to reliability problems and higher electricity costs. Members also asked what DOE, ERC, Transco, NAPOCOR, and NEA would do, and what documents or project updates they would provide.
agency_position: DOE and its attached agencies said that generation and transmission constraints were being addressed through project prioritization, third-party construction, island and Visayas master planning, storage, system-operations improvements, and coordination with NGCP. ERC maintained that LLCC suspension applied only during specified congested trading intervals and said it would review disputed collections. Several matters, including the Eastern Samar and Negros-Panay upgrades, remained subject to funding, approvals, NGCP implementation, or further study.
outcome: The hearing produced multiple agency commitments to evaluate allocations, submit documents, study or accelerate transmission projects, review LLCC collections, and provide NGCP performance information. However, the major transmission projects and the LLCC dispute remained dependent on approvals, funding, NGCP implementation, or further review.

positions.position: Iligan should receive a fair and practical increase in firm or non-firm power allocation because it hosts major power assets and consumers faced high rates.
Congress should carefully scrutinize new private distribution franchises, particularly where a small-capital entrant could enter the area of a well-performing cooperative.
Catanduanes needed an emergency response to high diesel-based generation costs and a long-term transmission interconnection, potentially including a submarine cable.
Eastern Samar required urgent 69 kV and northern-line upgrades, and ERC needed to clarify and correct the continued collection of LLCC after suspension.
Off-grid solar, reliable fuel allocation, pole-relocation funding, resilient island connections, and faster Visayas transmission upgrades were needed to reduce outages and line-rental costs.
DOE and NEA should prioritize electrification and host-community benefits in high-poverty areas, while maintaining offshore wind as part of the country's long-term energy mix.
Congress should obtain accountability and performance information on NGCP, accelerate Negros-Panay and related transmission projects, and address the grid's capacity to absorb renewable energy.

thread.speaker: Rep. Celso Regencia
thread.said: He raised rising electricity costs and supply stability in Iligan City, stating that the local charge increased from 13.6 per kilowatt hour in July 2026 to MXN 15.13 per kilowatt hour in August, an increase of MXN 1.52 or 11.19%.

thread.speaker: Rep. Celso Regencia
thread.said: He said Iligan hosted Agus-Pulangui assets with combined dependable capacity of approximately 279 megawatt, but firm allocation to Iligan Light and Power had been reduced to 8.75 megawatt.

thread.speaker: Rep. Celso Regencia
thread.said: He asked why Iligan's firm allocation had been reduced to 8.75 megawatt and whether the assessment considered actual demand, supply needs, and consumer impact. He also asked whether an additional 16.25 megawatt could be provided, restoring the allocation to 25 megawatt as an interim measure.

thread.speaker: PISAM official
thread.said: The official said PISAM reevaluated its supply contracts in 2026 and reduced cooperative allocations because the dependable capacity of Agus and Pulangui had declined. Allocations were based on the actual capacity of the power plants.

thread.speaker: PISAM official
thread.said: The official committed that PISAM and its trading team would evaluate Iligan Light and Power's request and try to increase its firm, or if necessary non-firm, allocation.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: The administrator agreed that a congressional franchise was indispensable for an electric cooperative to operate and distribute power. Functioning cooperatives, except in extreme cases, should be supported in franchise renewal.

thread.speaker: Congressman DiCasson
thread.said: He asked whether the generation market and transmission sector were competitive or monopolistic. The agency answered that EPIRA was intended to make generation competitive, while transmission operated under the franchise of NGCP as a sole operator.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official said transmission was under a franchise granted to NGCP and that there was only one operator. Distribution utilities and electric cooperatives had exclusive franchises in their respective areas.

thread.speaker: Congressman DiCasson
thread.said: He asked whether DOE had a division or bureau that conducted feasibility studies on the entry of a new private distribution utility and its economic impact on a local area.

thread.speaker: Electric Power Industry Management Bureau official
thread.said: The official said the bureau monitored distribution utilities, including cooperatives, through distribution development plans and power supply procurement programs. It monitored private utilities but did not assess an incoming new franchise holder.

thread.speaker: Congressman DiCasson
thread.said: He asked whether a private distribution company with paid-up capital of only 5,000,000 would have to build its own lines, substations, and transformers or could interconnect with or acquire an existing cooperative's facilities.

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon
thread.said: The Secretary said DOE could not approve or reject a franchise because that power belonged to Congress. Once granted, the franchise holder would have responsibility to deliver the public utility service, including putting up required infrastructure.

thread.speaker: Congressman DiCasson
thread.said: He asked whether it was fair to allow an unproven private distribution company with 5,000,000 paid-up capital to enter the franchise area of a triple-A cooperative that was performing well.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said NEA would defer to Congress on whether to grant a new franchise, but said the existing cooperative was performing well and should not be given up on. He cited improvement from more than 1,000,000,000 to 120,000,000 and its triple-A rating.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked DOE to support an emergency arrangement or temporary subsidy for Catanduanes because diesel generation costs and fuel prices were driving electricity rates, while also pursuing a long-term supply solution through competitive selection.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official said DOE could not commit to a subsidy because it was not authorized to provide one. DOE would instead form a task force, assess the cooperative and diesel supply, work with NAPOCOR, and pursue a longer-term reduction in diesel dependence.

thread.speaker: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez
thread.said: He asked for a long-term transmission solution for Catanduanes, including the transmission development plan, an interconnection project, a submarine cable, regulatory approvals, engineering services, and right-of-way work.

thread.speaker: Transco/NGCP official
thread.said: The official confirmed that the Catanduanes connection was included in NGCP's transmission development plan and could be prioritized. Transco would begin system operations on the island, which was expected to improve reliability and possibly reduce costs.

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon
thread.said: The Secretary said DOE had issued a circular allowing third-party construction, subject to coordination with NGCP. Transco had identified three projects and would work with NGCP and DOE to advance them.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: He asked how many megawatts were unavailable from the affected power plants during the outage and alert period.

thread.speaker: Agency official
thread.said: The official said each unit of TVI was one seventy six, with the unit of measurement unclear in the transcript, and that the outage reduced available supply and contributed to yellow and red alerts.

thread.speaker: Rep. Presley de Jesus
thread.said: He asked why line rentals had been suspended during congestion and how the resulting allocations would be corrected.

thread.speaker: ERC official
thread.said: The official said that when the Visayas-Mindanao interconnection was congested and line rentals spiked, ERC asked the market operator to suspend calculation and collection and collect only necessary amounts from customers and generators. ERC also sought recalculation and a third-party audit of payments and NSS allocations from 2021 onward to determine whether refunds were needed.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: Based on audit and monitoring records as of 06/20/2026, the official said remittances for Northern Luzon totaled 1,800,000,000, including 762,000,000 for electrification, 524,000,000 for the development fund, and 526,000,000 for watershed and rural health.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official said National Capital Region benefits totaled 8,000,000, including 4.44500000, 2,000,000 for DLF, and almost 2,000,000 for water management. The transcript's first NCR figure is unclear.

thread.speaker: Committee chair
thread.said: The chair asked the agency to submit the host-community remittance and audit information to the committee, and the agency agreed.

thread.speaker: Transco official
thread.said: The official said there were roughly 160,000 pending right-of-way claims, largely because of difficulties settling compensation and court processes.

thread.speaker: Transco official
thread.said: The official said Transco would begin an outsourced nationwide right-of-way settlement program, targeting 50,000 claims in two years and aiming to clear all claims by 2034 before the NGCP concession agreement ends.

thread.speaker: Transco official
thread.said: The official estimated the total cost of settling the claims at 220,000,000,000, based on a 2016 zonal valuation, while noting that unregistered and public land would not be paid for.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: Responding to Rep. Marco Anko's question on the Transco-NGCP dispute, the official said DOE continued to respect the concession agreement and was implementing the arbitral ruling issued in February 2025.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Anko
thread.said: He requested that DOE and Transco submit a written explanation of the matters involving NGCP and Transco, with a copy furnished to him.

thread.speaker: DOE and Transco officials
thread.said: The officials agreed to comply with the committee's request for a written explanation.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Anko
thread.said: He requested DOE's feasibility study on PNPP Unit One, saying the study was needed for House Bill 8567 and policy decisions on PNPP1 and future nuclear plants. He also submitted a copy of the subpoena that had been prepared but not served.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official said the hard copy of the feasibility study would be submitted to the committee by Friday or Monday, subject to the agreement with KHNP.

thread.speaker: Rep. Marco Anko
thread.said: He objected that the committee might receive a different copy from Korea and insisted on the exact copy held by DOE.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official explained that a confidentiality agreement prohibited photocopying or transmitting DOE's existing copy because the study had been provided as a KHNP grant. The official agreed to compare the incoming copy with DOE's copy and certify it.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sheen Gonzales
thread.said: He asked for the status of the Eastern Samar 69 kV sub-transmission line project, which was intended to address brownouts and low voltage.

thread.speaker: DOE/Transco official
thread.said: The official said the technical and financial feasibility study was ready and the project was awaiting DBM downloading and approval by the Office of the President. The line was described as close to 200 kilometers.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sheen Gonzales
thread.said: He also asked about upgrading the northern area's 128 kV line, which served three or four municipalities experiencing low voltage.

thread.speaker: DOE/Transco official
thread.said: The official said the northern upgrade would be prioritized through an investment fund for sustainable capital expenditure. The Secretary also directed Transco to study the transmission lines and visit the area.

thread.speaker: Rep. Sheen Gonzales
thread.said: He asked why LLCC or line rental charges continued after the ERC's August 5, 2026 suspension, citing an August 25, 2026 letter from the Independent Electricity Market Operator.

thread.speaker: ERC Commissioner Jan Rurik Padiernos
thread.said: The Commissioner explained that ERC's August 13, 2026 order suspended line-rental imposition only during trading intervals when congestion existed in the major Visayas-Mindanao interconnection. Line rentals could still be imposed during other intervals, and ERC would examine the specific case with the market operator.

thread.speaker: ERC official
thread.said: The ERC committed to look into the matter and resolve the issue.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: He asked whether funding for an approved off-grid solar plant would be included in the FY 2027 budget.

thread.speaker: DOE and NEA officials
thread.said: The officials said they would discuss the project with the member, verify whether it was under TEP funding, and follow through on the funding.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: He raised inadequate fuel allocation for an island that could provide 24-hour power and said he would submit the island's name in a letter.

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon
thread.said: The Secretary said NAPOCOR could determine whether the island was a SPUG area and redesign the supply arrangement to reduce dependence on diesel.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: He said an electric cooperative had already spent about 13,000,000 since 2023 for pole removal and relocation caused by road widening.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said NEA had requested at least 300,000,000 for cooperative pole-relocation advances, while 2026 DPWH allocation was 50,000,000.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: He asked whether a nearby island connection approximately 1.5 kilometers from the mainland could be converted to a submarine cable to improve resilience to typhoons.

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon
thread.said: The Secretary said a submarine cable was possible but required a cost-benefit analysis. DOE would check the option and consider another technology if the submarine cable was not economically viable.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: He said a European Union-donated solar project had received roughly 60,000,000 and asked whether monthly fees of roughly 100,000 could be waived.

thread.speaker: DOE and NEA officials
thread.said: DOE said NEA would check the status of the request. NEA said the fees might be needed for operation and maintenance but would examine how to address the request.

thread.speaker: Rep. Stephen James Tan
thread.said: He asked about the Luzon-Visayas transmission upgrade, citing power-shedding and high line-rental concerns in Regions 8 and 6. He said the planned upgrade was reportedly scheduled for 2032.

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon
thread.said: The Secretary said DOE was developing a Visayas master plan that would examine whether major islands should become more independent in meeting their energy needs rather than relying continuously on Luzon-Visayas-Mindanao interconnections. The initial major islands identified were Panay, Negros, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte, and Samar.

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon
thread.said: The Secretary said Panay had at one point paid about 3 pesos per line rental and said the Visayas master plan would be presented after further analysis, with the transcript indicating October.

thread.speaker: NAPOCOR President Coco Nograles
thread.said: He said the island had sufficient generators but was operating for only eight hours. NAPOCOR would study the economics of expanding service; current peak demand was 108 kilowatts.

thread.speaker: Rep. John Chan
thread.said: He asked how NEA would apply the proposed budget's poverty-prioritization provision and how many 2027 energization projects would be located in areas with the highest poverty counts. He cited 1,735,690 poor Filipinos and 279,220 poor families in Bicol.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said funding was directed particularly to geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, with the majority of the relevant funding dedicated to Mindanao. NEA was also working on allocations for Region 5, including Albay, but did not provide exact figures.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator
thread.said: The administrator said national electrification had increased from 75% to 89% in electric-cooperative franchise areas.

thread.speaker: Rep. John Chan
thread.said: He asked about the plan to increase ER 194 benefits from 1% to 3% for communities hosting geothermal plants, particularly in Region 5.

thread.speaker: DOE Secretary Sharon
thread.said: The Secretary clarified that the increase was from one centavo per kilowatt hour to three centavos, not from 1% to 3%. DOE had also loosened utilization rules and revised competitive-selection-process guidelines to give the host cooperative the right of first refusal.

thread.speaker: NEA administrator

topic: Electric-cooperative franchises, CBA obligations, and distribution competition
summary: Rep. Perci Cendaña pressed NEA on the suspended electric-cooperative CBA memorandum and asked whether it would be rescinded. NEA said a tripartite technical working group was developing rules and that the memorandum could be rescinded after a September 10 meeting and subsequent resolutions, but Cendaña noted that the same answer had been given the previous year. Rep. DiCasson questioned franchise expirations in 2028 or 2029, the exclusivity of cooperative distribution areas, and the suitability of a private applicant with 5,000,000 in capital compared with a cooperative with about 1,500,000,000 in assets. NEA and DOE said Congress controlled franchise grants, while functioning cooperatives generally merited renewal and franchise holders had to provide the required infrastructure and service. Rep. Sergio Dagooc raised labor demands including grocery allowances of up to 6,000 pesos monthly and laundry allowances of 500 to 600 pesos monthly, which NEA said cooperatives could not afford. ERC said new system-loss rules could support consumers or cooperative infrastructure and committed to propose revisions and consult stakeholders, including Mindanao cooperatives.
question: The committee sought to establish how the DOE, NEA, DOLE, and other agencies would resolve electric-cooperative collective-bargaining disputes and whether a memorandum affecting cooperative CBAs would be rescinded. It also examined the necessity of cooperative franchises, the possible entry of private distribution utilities, and whether revised system-loss rules could support cooperatives and consumers.
agency_position: The agencies maintained that the CBA memorandum was suspended because electric cooperatives had industry-specific circumstances, but said it could be rescinded after the tripartite council adopted resolutions. They supported renewal of functioning cooperative franchises, deferred franchise-grant decisions to Congress, warned that excessive CBA benefits could undermine cooperative finances, and said revised system-loss rules could allow consumer subsidies or infrastructure support subject to stakeholder consultation.
outcome: The CBA memorandum remained suspended, with possible rescission deferred until the tripartite council produced resolutions; Rep. Cendaña remained dissatisfied with the delay. The agencies supported functioning cooperatives and committed to consultation and possible revisions on system-loss rules, but the record did not resolve whether any new private franchise would be granted.

topic: ERC rate-setting, WESM overcharges, refunds, and consumer protection
summary: The ERC said it had directed refunds of around 71.3 billion and attributed 70 billion to Meralco's delayed rate reset, but Rep. Chukwish sought the exact WESM overcharge and a clearer refund account. The ERC responded with a technical explanation of locational marginal pricing, congestion, line losses, and settlement-surplus allocation, while referring to interim measures, a longer-term market-operator solution, and a third-party audit. Rep. Robert Nassal questioned why consumers paid for projected capital investments before completion and called for independent verification that charges funded useful investments. The ERC said it had shifted to performance-based regulation, using forecast costs, capital expenditure, returns, depreciation, and regulatory-asset-base calculations over four- or five-year periods. The ERC also sought around 200,000,000 plus for consulting services and related MOE to complete all utility rate resets in 2027, and Rep. Rufus Rodriguez said the request was approved according to the chairman. NEA separately requested 7 or 10 billion to cushion electric cooperatives from eliminating nontechnical system losses.
question: The committee sought to establish how the ERC set distribution-utility rates, including whether consumers were charged for projected investments before completion, and how WESM pricing flaws and market-settlement surpluses would be addressed through refunds. It also examined the ERC's budget needs for completing rate resets and supporting system-loss reduction.
agency_position: The ERC said it was implementing performance-based, forward-looking rate regulation while limiting recovery to approved asset values, returns, depreciation, and other recognized revenue-requirement components. It maintained that rate resets, WESM settlement measures, audits, and consumer-focused regulation were needed to protect consumers, but the transcript did not provide a clear exact WESM overcharge or refund amount.
outcome: The ERC answered the rate-setting question by explaining its performance-based methodology and said recovery was tied to approved asset values and regulatory-period resets. The exact WESM overcharge and refund requested by Rep. Chukwish remained unclear in the transcript, while the ERC's rate-reset funding request was stated to have been approved according to the chairman.

topic: System-loss VAT and consumer billing implementation
summary: Rep. Chukwish asked ERC Chair Francis Wang to clarify the treatment of the 12% VAT on system-loss charges and when consumers would see it in their bills. The ERC and DOE said implementation required BIR coordination, publication and effectivity steps, classification of technical and nontechnical losses, and phased work by electric cooperatives. Secretary Sharon said cooperatives would need about six months to prepare technical-loss plans and described 25% reduction stages toward eliminating nontechnical losses, with a possible report in the first half of the following year. Wang later identified September as the target for the BIR and billing-format process and said November was the earliest implementation after resolving September and October issues. An agency official cited 200,000,000 in support of the ERC budget because of the technical demands of the work.
question: The committee sought to establish the ERC's position on applying 12% VAT to system-loss charges and when consumers would see the treatment reflected in their bills. It also sought a timetable for reducing system losses and implementing the related billing changes.
agency_position: The DOE and ERC said the 12% VAT and system-loss billing treatment required coordination with the BIR, classification of technical and nontechnical losses, and a phased implementation rather than an immediate across-the-board reduction. They presented September as the target for the BIR and billing-format process, with November identified as the earliest implementation after resolving September and October issues.
outcome: The agencies provided a target timetable but acknowledged that billing and reconciliation issues remained. The issue therefore landed with an agency implementation plan and November as the earliest stated implementation point, rather than as an immediate consumer-billing change.

Rep. Reneko questioned incentives affecting indigenous communities and the environmental classification of waste-to-energy; the DOE cited prior informed consent, emissions safeguards, and the statutory classification but said it lacked authority to reclassify the technology. It favored safeguards and stronger generator accountability rather than direct generation-cost regulation, and said it could not reclassify waste-to-energy without a change in the law.
outcome: The DOE's renewable-energy expansion plans were presented as supported by auctions, new project types, and consumer-access programs, but questions about agricultural-land protection, hydrological review, contract cancellations, indigenous safeguards, and waste-to-energy records remained subject to further review or reporting. topic: Catanduanes and island high-cost generation assistance
summary: Rep. Rufus Rodriguez sought an emergency subsidy and long-term transmission solution for Catanduanes, where diesel dependence was driving high electricity costs. DOE declined to commit to a subsidy but promised a task force, fuel and electric-cooperative assessment, coordination with NAPOCOR, and work toward a grid connection or other long-term solution. Rep. Stephen James Tan then raised funding for an off-grid solar project, fuel allocation for an island system, pole relocation, a submarine-cable option, solar-plant fee relief, and the Luzon-Visayas transmission upgrade. The agencies cited about 300 million requested for pole-relocation advances, 50 million in a 2026 DPWH allocation, roughly 60 million in donated solar support, and roughly 100,000 a month in fees, while NAPOCOR said one island was operating at eight hours with peak demand stated unclearly as “a 100 kilo 108 kilowatts.” The issues were not finally resolved, but DOE, NEA, Transco, and NAPOCOR undertook follow-up studies, coordination, and presentations.

agency_position: DOE and its attached agencies did not commit to a temporary subsidy, saying DOE was not authorized to support one. topic: Ancillary services, stranded costs, and excess renewable capacity
summary: A majority member asked the ERC to address stranded costs that could arise when distribution utilities retained excess contracted capacity while consumers shifted toward solar power. The ERC pointed to carve-out provisions in post-2023 power-supply agreements and said it would examine assistance for utilities and captive customers. A member also questioned ancillary charges, stating that about 60 percent of transmission charges were ancillary charges and citing a reserve-market price of 25 pesos per kilowatt hour; the ERC said a lower-price proposal was under consultation. Javi Benitez connected transmission delays in Negros and Panay to possible renewable curtailment involving roughly 1,300 megawatts of projects, with risks described as about 10% and possibly 20% to 30%, while DOE cited 50 megawatts of proposed battery storage in Negros. A minority member pressed for CSP amendments, greater NGCP accountability for ancillary services, and solar-plus-storage in place of uneconomic line extensions, citing 200,000,000 for the proposed funding step. The matters were not finally resolved, but the ERC and DOE undertook further review and reporting.
question: The committee sought to establish how stranded costs from excess or curtailed renewable capacity would be allocated, whether distribution utilities and consumers could be protected from those costs, and whether ancillary-service and reserve-market charges could be reduced and made more accountable. It also examined whether transmission constraints were contributing to renewable curtailment and whether solar-plus-storage could substitute for uneconomic line extensions.
agency_position: The ERC said existing and post-2023 power-supply agreements could use carve-outs or other mechanisms to unload excess contracted capacity, and it was considering a reserve-market proposal intended to lower pricing. DOE said transmission was lagging generation, supported battery storage as an alternative or supplement, and would monitor and report on NGCP transmission commitments.
outcome: The ERC described existing contractual and reserve-market mechanisms for excess capacity and undertook to consider a proposal intended to reduce reserve-market prices. Transmission-related curtailment, ancillary-service accountability, and the proposed CSP and solar-plus-storage changes remained open for further action.

Battery storage, including a proposed 50 megawatts in Negros, could help manage excess renewable power and transmission constraints.

summary: Rep. Presley De Jesus asked the DOE for the total ER 194 host-community remittances and questioned the apparent gap in benefits. topic: Nuclear-energy roadmap, SMR feasibility, and regulatory framework
summary: Rep. Marco Anko pressed the DOE over the PNPP Unit 1 feasibility study, saying it was needed for House bill eight five six seven and other nuclear-policy decisions. The DOE said the study was controlled under its agreement with KHNP and could not be photocopied or transmitted, but committed to submit the arriving hard copy by Monday and compare and certify it against the DOE-held version. Rep. Tino then asked about the status, technology, cost, and providers for Philippine nuclear development. Secretary Sharon said the country had a roadmap and a target for nuclear energy in the next decade, but was reconsidering SMRs in favor of conventional technology because SMR options appeared limited. She said regulatory organization and implementing rules remained to be completed, and gave indicative costs of 10,000,000,000 for conventional technology and 4,000,000,000 for an SMR. The DOE said development would rely mostly on private funding and that it was exploring providers from Korea, China, Japan, Canada, the United States, and France.
question: The committee sought to establish the status and availability of the DOE's PNPP Unit 1 feasibility study, including whether the committee would receive the same document held by the DOE. It also asked about the country's nuclear roadmap, the choice between small modular reactors (SMRs) and conventional reactors, regulatory readiness, technology providers, and indicative costs.
agency_position: The DOE said the Philippines had a nuclear roadmap and still targeted nuclear energy in the next decade, but was reconsidering an SMR-centered approach because options appeared limited and conventional technology might be pursued instead. The agency said regulatory and safety requirements were still being completed, nuclear development would rely mostly on private funding, and technology and provider options remained under study.
outcome: The feasibility-study issue landed on a commitment for the DOE to submit the copy arriving from Korea by Monday and to compare and certify it against the DOE-held copy. The broader nuclear roadmap remained exploratory: the DOE had not settled the SMR-versus-conventional choice, regulatory framework, provider, or financing arrangement.

topic: Offshore-wind development and supporting port and grid infrastructure
summary: Rep. Jan Franz Chan asked whether the cited target of 21 gigawatts by 2040, or about 21% of national electricity, remained the administration's working offshore-wind target. The DOE secretary said offshore wind continued to be promoted but did not confirm the 21% figure, pending a new energy-mix simulation expected at the end of the year. A DOE undersecretary said an offshore-wind auction covering 3,300 megawatts was ongoing. Chan then asked about budget support for port works and grid preparation. The Philippine Ports Authority said offshore-wind ports would require about 30 tons per square meter, compared with six to eight tons for existing ports, and identified projects in Pambuhan and Santa Clara, with stated construction timelines. Curimao Port was described as intended for floating offshore wind and not to be contracted under the current administration because the auction mainly covered fixed-bottom projects. No specific budget amount for grid preparation was committed, but the port project timelines and DOE's year-end energy-mix update were stated.

topic: DOE special-fund authority and retained agency income
summary: Rep. Robert Nassal asked whether the proposed 20% authority would ensure DOE access to PD number 910 earmarked funds and what programs would be financed. Secretary Sharon Garin said DOE did not receive the full statutory share because GOCCs were also covered, but identified automation, grid management, regional facilities, green buildings, and energy research as potential uses. She projected that 20% of 2027 Malampaya collections could be about 5.4 billion. DOE officials said more than 2 million households remained without electricity and that about 10 billion a year would be needed for electrification, compared with current annual funding of about 2 billion to 3 billion. Later, DOE requested authority to retain 3% for administrative and engineering costs, but the chair said DBM had previously found no legal basis for similar requests. The committee requested prioritized lists and supporting details by the following day and deferred the legal issue for discussion with DBM before plenary.
question: The committee sought to establish whether the proposed 20% special-fund authority would allow DOE to access legally earmarked PD Number 910 funds, what programs would be financed, and whether the additional fiscal space could accelerate total electrification. outcome: The committee generally supported DOE's access to legally earmarked funds and the need for higher electrification resources, but required program details and prioritized special-provision language. The retained-income request was not resolved during the hearing and was deferred for consultation with DBM before plenary.

thread.said: Rep. Nassal asked whether improved access to earmarked funds, assuming 4,000,000,000, could be used to accelerate total electrification. He asked how many CTOs and households remained without electricity as of 08/31/2026 and how much it would cost to electrify all of them.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin pointed to DOE's Total Electrification Program and the NAES budget, and asked that the impact of increasing the program to 2,000,000,000 or so be considered.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: A DOE official said the current total electrification program budget was 500,000,000 per year and that more than 2,000,000 households remained without electricity.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official cited 100,000,000,000 pesos every year, 10,000,000,000 a year, and a range of two to 3,000,000,020.22, followed by references to 2028, 2038, and 2043 electrification computations. The statement is garbled and its intended figures are unclear.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal asked how much would be needed annually beginning in 2028.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The DOE official answered that 2028 would require 10,000,000,000 a year from government, while DOE was receiving only about 2,000,000,000 to 3,000,000,000 per year.

thread.speaker: Rep. Robert Nassal
thread.said: Rep. Nassal supported increasing the electrification budget and reiterated that DOE should have access to its earmarked funds.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing asked DOE and ERC to identify programs and projects not funded in the NEP that they wanted the budget amendments review subcommittee to consider, including requested special provisions.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin said most of DOE's requested items would not involve additional funding. She identified proposed provisions concerning electric vehicles and a separate request involving administrative costs, but the transcript is unclear on the exact wording of the latter.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin referred to a special provision on the use of 55% for administrative purposes, after which another speaker corrected the figure to 3%. The transcript is unclear on the precise provision.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: She referred to a request allowing CPNOC to reserve 8,000,000,000 in corporate funds for construction of a facility, and said the request would not involve additional funding.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin said DOE had collected 6,000,000,000 pesos from Malampaya that year and expected next year's collections to increase to about 27,000,000,000. She said the increase was about 21,000,000,000 and that the funds would go to the national coffers; the statement also contains an unclear reference to 200,000,000.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: A DOE-related official asked whether a 3% executive and administrative cost could be kept as general income of Naya to cover additional engineers needed to inspect and certify solar home system projects.

thread.speaker: DOE official
thread.said: The official said the agency was struggling to implement the project on time and needed additional manpower. The request was to use EIO for salaries and wages of additional personnel; the transcript does not clearly identify the acronym or entity.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing said the committee would confer with DBM because a similar ERC request to use retained income had been rejected in the previous year. She said DBM's position was that there was no legal basis to allow such use.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing said the committee would obtain DBM's position on the retained-income request and address the legal complexity separately rather than wait for a DBM representative during the hearing.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing said the committee would settle the special-provision issue after conferring with DBM, Secretary Garin, and the vice chair, preferably before the matter reached plenary.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing requested a prioritized list of DOE's proposed special provisions and other items by the end of the week, ultimately specifying submission by tomorrow, so the subcommittee could deliberate on them.

thread.speaker: Chair Mika Suansing
thread.said: Chair Suansing extended the request for detailed information to ERC, including the details supporting its additional requirements and proposed special provisions.

thread.speaker: Secretary Sharon Garin
thread.said: Secretary Garin agreed to coordinate on the requested submissions and special-provision language.
